analysis.one_liner: Restores overtime pay to salaried managers earning under about $57,000 a year.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2014, the bill was referred to the Senate labor committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal labor law lets employers skip paying overtime to workers they classify as executives, administrators, or professionals, and employers use that 'exempt' label to assign salaried employees manager titles while paying them low wages and working them long hours. This bill would set a salary floor below which no one can be denied overtime — starting at about $34,580 and rising to about $56,680 over three years, then adjusting with inflation. It would also require that exempt workers spend most of their time doing exempt-level duties, and would fine employers that repeatedly or willfully falsify or fail to keep wage and hour records.
analysis.who_benefits: Salaried workers earning below the new thresholds who are currently labeled 'exempt' and work more than 40 hours a week without overtime — restaurant and retail managers, low-level supervisors, and office staff given manager titles. They would either collect overtime pay or work fewer hours.

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets a salary threshold below which employees cannot be classified as exempt, starting at $665 per week (about $34,580 a year), rising to $865 and then $1,090 per week (about $56,680 a year) over three years, then adjusting annually with the Consumer Price Index [S3].

It adds a 'primary duty' rule: an employee classified as exempt cannot spend more than 50 percent of their weekly hours on non-exempt duties, closing the practice of paying a low wage for mostly non-managerial work while withholding overtime [S3].
It sets a higher compensation level for the separate 'highly compensated employee' exemption, rising from $108,000 to $125,000 over three years and then indexing to inflation [S3].

It makes the existing civil penalty apply to employers who repeatedly or willfully violate the requirement to make and keep accurate records of employees' wages and hours — the records on which any overtime claim depends [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers in retail, restaurants, banking, insurance, and other industries that rely on salaried exempt workers would pay overtime or reclassify workers to hourly with overtime, adding payroll costs. Some might cut hours, base pay, or hire fewer people to offset it.

drawbacks.text: Employers would face real added payroll costs and compliance work, and small businesses operating on thin margins in low-margin industries would feel it most [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that employers can respond to a higher overtime bar in ways workers don't want: cutting base pay, limiting hours, or converting salaried positions to rigid hourly ones that remove schedule flexibility [S3].

The 50 percent duties rule is a bright line, and some employees who do genuinely split work between managing and doing would be reclassified to hourly even when both they and the employer prefer the salaried arrangement [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete: millions of salaried workers under the new thresholds would gain overtime rights that a low salary and a manager title currently erase, and the inflation adjustment keeps the threshold from eroding the way past rule changes did. The cost falls on employers, chiefly in low-wage service industries, and is partly passed through as scheduling changes. The main design weakness is the rigid 50 percent duty test, which will classify some borderline workers in ways that suit neither side. On balance the bill transfers pay to workers with little power to negotiate overtime terms.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in June 2014 and sent to the Senate committee that handles labor law, and it sat there — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — until Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin introduced the bill on June 18, 2014, joined by seven Democratic senators and one Independent; no Republican signed on [S3][S4].
That same day the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, which took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2015, and the bill died in committee without ever reaching the Senate floor [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have owed overtime to salaried managers earning under the new thresholds keep the current exemption unchanged, saving the payroll costs the bill would have imposed.

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Iowa; sponsor of the bill and chairman of the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the labor committee, which he chaired; the committee held no hearing or markup on it

for.name: Sens. Murray, Sanders, Casey, Warren, Leahy, Boxer, Brown, and Markey
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors on the day of introduction

against.name: 45 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None cosponsored the bill; with the chamber short of the 60 votes needed to overcome a routine delay tactic, the bill never reached the floor

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: The Senate committee with jurisdiction over labor law
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill in and never scheduled a hearing or vote on it before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's one Independent; not a single Republican senator signed on, and the bill never advanced past committee referral.

industries.industry: Employers of salaried exempt workers (retail, restaurants, banking, insurance, and other low-wage service employers)
industries.note: These employers currently use low salaries and manager titles to avoid paying overtime; the bill would force them to pay time-and-a-half over 40 hours or reclassify workers, a direct payroll cost that comes out of what workers would otherwise absorb as unpaid hours.
Small employers with thin margins would bear compliance and payroll costs like larger ones, though the workers whose hours they manage are the bill's beneficiaries.
